title: Divisibility
coreInsight: Divisibility asks whether a quantity can be partitioned into equal groups with no remainder; digit tests are consequences of place-value structure rather than magic rules.
targetLearnerRealization: Divisibility means forming equal groups with no remainder; familiar digit tests are shortcuts that come from place-value structure rather than arbitrary rules.
learningObjectives: Interpret divisibility as equal grouping with remainder zero.
Use divisor, factor, and multiple with distinct meanings.
Explain divisibility tests for 2, 5, 10, and 9 from place value.
Use a digit test only under its justified condition and retain remainder information.

continuity.openingCallback: Move from estimating a quantity's size to asking whether it lands exactly on an equal-group boundary.
closingSeeds: Prime factorization repeatedly splits a composite number into divisors.
Divisibility is the remainder-zero case of a broader remainder system.
Odd/even parity records only the remainder after division by 2.

misconceptionTargets.misconception: Divisor, factor, and multiple are interchangeable words.
A divisibility test can be applied outside the condition under which it was derived.
The remainder can be ignored when discussing divisibility.

beats.purpose: Create the need for remainder zero by comparing candidate totals under equal grouping.
beats.expectedRealization: Only a total landing exactly on a six-group boundary can be split with no leftovers.
beats.transitionIn: A magnitude estimate locates a number roughly. Equal grouping asks a sharper question: does the number land exactly on a boundary?
beats.transitionOut: Thirty-six worked because six complete groups used every tile; the other totals left unfinished groups.
beats.whyNow: A concrete grouping puzzle establishes meaning before vocabulary or digit shortcuts.
beats.entryBridge: Try to form groups of six and keep any leftover tiles visible.
beats.exitBridge: Six groups of six use all 36 tiles, so the remainder is zero.
beats.reusedRepresentation: Tiles arranged as complete equal groups with leftovers separated.
learnerPrompts: How many complete groups of six form?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct—36 makes six complete groups of six with no leftovers.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Divide each choice by 6 and keep the remainder visible.

visual.ariaLabel: Thirty-six tiles arranged into six equal groups of six with no leftovers

steps.body: The equation 36 = 6 × 6 uses every tile. A remainder of zero is the decisive feature.

resolution.takeaway: Exact equal grouping means no remainder is left behind.

beats.purpose: Contrast a nearly complete grouping with true divisibility.
beats.expectedRealization: A positive remainder means the divisor does not divide the total exactly.
beats.transitionIn: Now move two tiles past that exact boundary.
beats.prompt: When 38 tiles are placed into groups of 6, six groups form and 2 tiles remain. Is 38 divisible by 6?

options.text: Yes, because six groups formed.
No, because the remainder is 2.
Yes, because 38 is close to 36.

beats.correctFeedback: Right—divisibility requires remainder zero, not merely some complete groups.
beats.incorrectFeedback: The two leftover tiles are part of the answer to the grouping question.

steps.body: 38 = 6 × 6 + 2. The remainder 2 proves the split is not exact.

resolution.takeaway: A number d divides n only when dividing n by d leaves remainder 0.

beats.purpose: Attach distinct relational roles to divisor, factor, and multiple.
beats.expectedRealization: In 6 × 6 = 36, 6 is a factor and divisor of 36, while 36 is a multiple of 6.
beats.transitionIn: The same exact grouping can be read in three directions. Keep track of which number acts on which.

options.text: 6 is a divisor and factor of 36; 36 is a multiple of 6.
36 is a divisor of 6; 6 is a multiple of 36.
Divisor and multiple are interchangeable names.
6 is the remainder of 36.

beats.correctFeedback: Exactly—factor and divisor point into the product; multiple points out to the product.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Ask which smaller number divides 36 exactly and which larger number appears in the multiplication list of 6.

steps.body: Because 36 = 6 × 6, each 6 is a factor of 36. Since 36 ÷ 6 has remainder zero, 6 is a divisor of 36. The product 36 is a multiple of 6.

resolution.takeaway: A divisor divides the number; a factor builds the number; a multiple is built from the factor.

beats.purpose: Name divisibility only after exact grouping and remainder have been experienced.
beats.expectedRealization: Divisibility is an exact relationship equivalent to a whole-number product and remainder zero.
beats.transitionIn: You have already identified the decisive condition: every object belongs to a complete equal group.
beats.name: Divisibility
beats.conciseDefinition: A whole number n is divisible by d when n can be written as d times a whole number, with no remainder.
beats.formalization: d divides n ⇔ n = d × q for a whole number q ⇔ n ÷ d has remainder 0

beats.purpose: Derive 2, 5, and 10 tests from the grouping behavior of tens.
beats.expectedRealization: All complete tens are divisible by 2, 5, and 10, so only the ones digit can change those divisibility decisions.
beats.transitionIn: Large numbers contain complete bundles of ten. For some divisors, every such bundle disappears into equal groups.
beats.prompt: Why can the ones digit decide divisibility by 2, 5, and 10?

options.text: Every group of 10 is divisible by 2, 5, and 10, so only leftover ones can affect the remainder.
The final digit is always the largest digit.
The digits always add to the number.
The ones digit decides divisibility by every divisor.

beats.correctFeedback: Right—tens contribute remainder zero for those three divisors.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Split a number into complete tens plus its ones digit and examine each divisor.

steps.body: Write n = 10q + r, where r is the ones digit. Because 10q is divisible by 2, 5, and 10, n has the same remainder behavior as r for those divisors.
This argument does not justify using only the ones digit for an arbitrary divisor.

resolution.takeaway: A digit test is a place-value shortcut whose valid divisor must be justified.

beats.purpose: Derive the digit-sum test for 9 from each power of ten leaving remainder one.
beats.expectedRealization: Modulo 9, each place-value unit contributes like one, so a number and its digit sum have the same remainder.
beats.transitionIn: For 9, tens do not disappear completely: each 10 is one more than a multiple of 9. That leftover one repeats at every place.
beats.prompt: Without dividing 372 by 9, what does its digit sum tell you?

options.text: 372 is divisible by 9 because its last digit is even.
372 is not divisible by 9 because 3 + 7 + 2 = 12 is not divisible by 9.
372 is divisible by 9 because 10 is close to 9.
A digit sum can never answer a divisibility question.

beats.correctFeedback: Correct—the digit sum leaves remainder 3 modulo 9, so the original number does too.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Use 100 ≡ 1 and 10 ≡ 1 modulo 9, so 372 has the same remainder as 3 + 7 + 2.

steps.body: Because 100 = 99 + 1 and 10 = 9 + 1, 3 hundreds, 7 tens, and 2 ones have the same remainder as 3 + 7 + 2.
The sum 12 = 9 + 3 leaves remainder 3, so 372 is not divisible by 9.

resolution.takeaway: Digit sums work for 9 because every base-ten place has remainder 1 when divided by 9.

beats.purpose: Apply a structurally explained divisibility condition to a missing digit.
beats.expectedRealization: Equal payment forces divisibility by 11, and the alternating digit balance determines A = 3.
beats.transitionIn: A digit test can become a constraint on an unknown digit. Here equal shares first tell us which divisor matters.
beats.transitionOut: The alternating difference forced A = 3, and direct division confirmed 132 = 11 × 12.
beats.whyNow: The approved problem converts equal grouping into an 11-divisibility digit constraint after digit tests have been treated as structural shortcuts.
beats.entryBridge: Translate equal payment by 11 people into remainder zero, then track how A changes the alternating digit difference.
beats.exitBridge: Only A = 3 makes 1 + 2 − A equal zero in the possible range.
beats.reusedRepresentation: Place-value digit tiles collapse into a smaller remainder calculation.
learnerPrompts: Why must the total be a multiple of 11?
What alternating difference do the digits produce?
Which digit makes that difference a multiple of 11?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct—A = 3 makes the total $132, or $12 per member.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Equal shares require a multiple of 11; test the alternating difference 1 + 2 − A.

steps.body: Eleven equal payments require the total 1A2 to be divisible by 11.
The alternating difference is 1 + 2 − A = 3 − A. For a digit A, only zero is a possible multiple of 11 in this range, so A = 3.
Check: 132 ÷ 11 = 12 with remainder zero.

resolution.takeaway: Use the condition to choose the divisor, then apply only the test justified for that divisor.

beats.purpose: Repair the classification of 1 before prime factorization begins.
beats.expectedRealization: One has only one positive divisor, so it is neither prime nor composite under the two-divisor definition.
beats.transitionIn: Factors describe how a number can be built. Before splitting numbers further, settle the smallest positive case.
beats.prompt: A prime number has exactly two positive divisors: 1 and itself. Why is 1 not prime?

options.text: Its list of positive divisors contains only 1, not two distinct divisors.
It is odd.
Every number below 10 is not prime.
It divides every whole number.

beats.correctFeedback: Exactly—1 has one positive divisor, not exactly two.

steps.body: The only positive divisor of 1 is 1. Prime numbers require two distinct positive divisors, so 1 is neither prime nor composite.

resolution.takeaway: Definitions depend on exact counts; “almost two divisors” is not prime.

beats.purpose: Combine a digit-sum divisibility constraint with a separate remainder computation.
beats.expectedRealization: The 9-test determines U = 7, but a new divisor requires a new justified shortcut and an explicit remainder.
beats.transitionIn: One number now faces two different divisors. Keep their tests separate instead of treating a digit trick as universal.
beats.transitionOut: The digit sum fixed 20187; the last three digits then left remainder 3 upon division by 8.
beats.whyNow: The approved transfer tests whether the learner chooses a test by divisor and preserves remainder information beyond the zero case.
beats.entryBridge: Use divisibility by 9 to find U, then start a fresh remainder-by-8 calculation on the completed number.
beats.exitBridge: Since 1000 is divisible by 8, only 187 affects the remainder, and 187 = 8 × 23 + 3.
beats.reusedRepresentation: Digit tiles first collapse to a sum, then a justified last-three-digit tail.
learnerPrompts: Which U makes the digit sum a multiple of 9?
Why is that rule finished once U is known?
Why do the last three digits control the remainder modulo 8?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct—U = 7 and 20187 leaves remainder 3 when divided by 8.
beats.incorrectFeedback: First make 11 + U a multiple of 9. Then divide the completed last three digits 187 by 8 and retain the remainder.

steps.body: The digit sum is 11 + U. The only digit making it a multiple of 9 is U = 7, giving 20187.
Because 1000 is divisible by 8, the leading 20 thousands contribute remainder zero. Compute with 187.
187 = 8 × 23 + 3, so the requested remainder is 3.

resolution.takeaway: Every divisor needs its own justification, and a nonzero remainder must stay in the conclusion.

beats.purpose: Assess exact grouping and quotient interpretation.
beats.expectedRealization: Fifty-two divides into thirteen groups of four with remainder zero.
beats.transitionIn: Return to physical grouping and report both exactness and group count.
beats.transitionOut: The equation 52 = 4 × 13 certifies divisibility and names the quotient.
beats.whyNow: A near item checks the foundation meaning without digit shortcuts.
beats.entryBridge: Form complete groups of four and record any remainder.
beats.exitBridge: Thirteen full boxes use all 52 balls.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Count by fours to 52 and check for leftovers.

steps.body: Since 4 × 13 = 52, all balls fill 13 boxes and none remain.

resolution.takeaway: A whole-number quotient and remainder zero certify divisibility.

beats.expectedRealization: Eight divides 56 exactly, so 8 is a divisor and factor while 56 is its multiple.
beats.transitionIn: Use one multiplication fact to read the relationship in both directions.
beats.transitionOut: The same equation supports different words because the numbers play different roles.
beats.whyNow: A near vocabulary item prevents relational language from drifting.
beats.exitBridge: Eight is a factor and divisor of 56; 56 is a multiple of 8.

steps.body: Because 56 = 8 × 7, 8 is a factor and divisor of 56, and 56 is a multiple of 8.

resolution.takeaway: Keep the direction of each divisibility word attached to an equation.

beats.purpose: Assess structural last-digit tests for 2, 5, and 10.
beats.expectedRealization: A final zero makes 3270 divisible by all three listed divisors.
beats.transitionIn: Now let complete tens handle the large part and inspect only the leftover ones digit.
beats.transitionOut: The final zero contributes remainder zero for 2, 5, and 10.
beats.whyNow: A mixed item coordinates three tests with a shared place-value reason.
learnerPrompts: Which divisors divide every complete ten?
What does the ones digit contribute?
beats.incorrectFeedback: A final zero can be grouped by 2, 5, or 10 with no remainder.

steps.body: The number is 327 complete tens with no extra ones. Ten is divisible by 2, 5, and 10, so the whole number is divisible by all three.

resolution.takeaway: The last-digit shortcut is justified by complete base-ten bundles.

beats.purpose: Assess a missing digit under the 9-divisibility condition.
beats.expectedRealization: The digit sum 6 + A must equal 9, forcing A = 3.
beats.transitionIn: Use the digit sum as a compact remainder calculation, not a memorized incantation.
beats.transitionOut: A = 3 makes 432's digit sum 9 and direct division confirms 48 groups of 9.
beats.whyNow: A mixed item mirrors the constraint form while using the previously derived 9-test rather than the bank problem's 11-test.
beats.entryBridge: Replace each place value by its remainder 1 modulo 9.
learnerPrompts: What is the known digit sum?
Which digit reaches a multiple of 9?
beats.incorrectFeedback: The digit sum is 4 + A + 2 = 6 + A; make it a multiple of 9.

steps.body: For digit A, 6 + A ranges from 6 through 15. The only multiple of 9 in that range is 9, so A = 3.
Check: 432 ÷ 9 = 48 with remainder zero.

resolution.takeaway: A digit test turns a whole-number divisibility condition into a smaller remainder constraint.

beats.purpose: Assess systematic search for the first shared divisible value.
beats.expectedRealization: Seventy-two is the first multiple of 8 above 50 that is also divisible by 6.
beats.transitionIn: For the final challenge, find a number that lands on two equal-group boundaries at once.
beats.transitionOut: Listing multiples in order proved both that 72 works and that no smaller value above 50 does.
beats.whyNow: The challenge combines divisibility meaning with a complete bounded search without requiring prime factorization.
beats.entryBridge: List multiples of 8 above 50 and test each for division by 6.
learnerPrompts: What are the first multiples of 8 above 50?
Which first has remainder zero when divided by 6?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct—72 is the least qualifying number.

steps.body: The multiples of 8 above 50 begin 56, 64, 72. The first two are not divisible by 6; 72 = 6 × 12.

resolution.takeaway: An ordered candidate list can prove a least common boundary.

beats.purpose: Consolidate meaning, language, test justification, and remainder discipline.
beats.expectedRealization: A sound divisibility claim connects exact grouping, correct relational language, and a justified shortcut.
beats.transitionIn: Groups, digits, payments, and remainders all point back to the same exact condition.
beats.prompt: Which checks belong in a reliable divisibility argument? Select all four.

options.text: Require remainder zero for a divisibility claim.
Confirm the number equals divisor × whole-number quotient.
Keep divisor/factor and multiple roles in the correct direction.
Use a digit test only for a divisor whose place-value behavior justifies it.
Ignore a small remainder if most groups are complete.

response.feedback: Keep exactness, product structure, word direction, and justified shortcuts.

beats.correctFeedback: Exactly—zero remainder, whole-number product, correct roles, and a justified test.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Any nonzero remainder means the division is not exact.

groups.label: Language
choices: d divides n; n is a multiple

resolution.takeaway: Complete groups, zero leftovers—and explain any shortcut.

beats.purpose: Create the successor question about numbers that cannot be split into smaller nontrivial factors.
beats.expectedRealization: Repeated factor splitting ends differently for prime and composite numbers, with 1 requiring separate treatment.
beats.transitionIn: Some numbers have many divisor pairs; others have no positive divisor except 1 and themselves.
beats.prompt: If you keep splitting 60 into factor pairs, which numbers should end the branches—and why must 1 not count as one of those prime endpoints?
beats.takeaway: Next, we will split composite numbers until every branch ends in a genuine prime factor.

notes: Draft foundation lesson authored from the approved N1 compact context packet.
Equal grouping creates the meaning before place-value shortcuts; both approved AMC problems then use divisor-specific digit reasoning.
Divisor/factor/multiple language, the status of 1, test conditions, and nonzero remainders are repaired explicitly.
All generated answers were independently checked by direct division and a separate product, enumeration, or remainder argument.
No lesson-specific renderer infrastructure was added.
